items.title: Plants can push water up — but only a few metres
items.claim: Roots actively pump ions into the xylem at night. Water follows by osmosis, generating pressure that pushes sap upward. You can see it as guttation: droplets of liquid forced out at leaf tips in the morning.
items.prompt: Why does root pressure not lift water all the way to a redwood canopy?

options.text: Root pressure rarely exceeds ~0.2 MPa — enough to push water ~20 metres. Taller transport requires transpiration-driven tension at the leaves (cohesion-tension theory)
Water cannot move upward in plants

items.reveal:
Two mechanisms drive xylem flow:

1. Root pressure (positive): active ion transport into xylem; water follows; positive pressure pushes sap upward. Works in small herbaceous plants, in young growing tissue, and in trees in early spring before leaves open. Maxes out at ~0.2 MPa.

2. Transpiration pull (tension, cohesion-tension theory): evaporation at leaves creates negative pressure; cohesive water column transmits the pull down to roots. Routinely reaches -1 to -2 MPa. Works in any tree height up to ~130 m.

Guttation is visible evidence of root pressure: drops of xylem sap forced out of hydathodes on leaf tips overnight (when stomata are closed and transpiration cannot relieve the pressure). Looks like dew but contains dissolved minerals.

Most mature trees rely entirely on transpiration pull. Root pressure becomes detectable only when transpiration is suppressed (humid nights, plant chopped down, etc.).

Notably, mosses lack vascular tissue entirely and rely on diffusion and capillary action — which is why they top out at ~20 cm.
items.why: Roots seem like obvious pumps. They are — but only weak ones. The real heavy lifting in tall plants is done by evaporation at the top, pulling on water held together by hydrogen bonds.

items.title: Sugar in plants flows from wherever it's made to wherever it's needed
items.claim: Xylem carries water in one direction: up. Phloem carries dissolved sugars in any direction — up, down, lateral — from 'sources' (leaves, storage organs being mobilised) to 'sinks' (roots, fruits, growing tips). The same phloem tube can reverse direction with the season.

options.text: Pressure-flow (Munch) hypothesis: sugar loaded at the source raises osmotic pressure there, drawing in water from xylem; unloaded sugar at the sink reduces pressure; bulk flow proceeds from high to low pressure along the phloem

items.reveal:
Phloem sieve tubes are living cells (unlike xylem vessels, which are dead). Companion cells help load sugar into sieve elements at sources.

Loading: at a source (e.g., a photosynthesising leaf), sucrose is actively pumped INTO sieve elements via H+/sucrose symporters. Sucrose concentration rises to 1 mol/L. Water enters by osmosis. Hydrostatic pressure builds.

Unloading: at a sink (a fruit, root, or growing meristem), sucrose is removed and metabolised or stored. Water exits. Pressure drops.

The pressure gradient pushes sap from source to sink at ~1 metre/hour — much slower than xylem flow but still bulk flow.

Direction reverses seasonally. In spring, a deciduous tree's stored root sugars are sources, mobilising to buds (sinks). In summer, leaves are sources, fruits and roots are sinks. In autumn, leaves dump sugars to storage organs before falling.

Aphids tap phloem with their stylets and benefit from the natural pressure — sap is forced out of them as honeydew. Scientists use severed aphid stylets as natural phloem sampling needles.
items.why: Plant transport feels static. The phloem is a dynamic, switchable distribution network with pressure-driven bulk flow — and it can reverse direction within a single growing season.

items.title: A woman who died in 1951 still has dividing cells today
items.claim: Normal human cells divide about 50 times and then stop (the Hayflick limit). HeLa cells, taken from Henrietta Lacks's cervical tumour in 1951, divide indefinitely. They are in laboratories on every continent.

options.text: Constitutive expression of telomerase — the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres on chromosome ends — allows them to divide without losing telomeric DNA, bypassing the Hayflick limit. The HPV-derived oncogenes E6 and E7 also disable normal tumour suppressors
Special preservation chemicals keep them alive
All cancer cells are technically immortal

items.reveal_title: Telomeres, telomerase, and the loophole around cell senescence
items.reveal:
Linear chromosomes lose a small amount of DNA from their ends with each replication (the 'end replication problem'). Once telomeres reach a critical short length, cells trigger senescence — the Hayflick limit, named after Leonard Hayflick (1961).

Most adult cells suppress telomerase. Germline cells, stem cells and most cancers reactivate it. HeLa cells express telomerase robustly. Combined with disabled tumour suppressors (p53 and Rb, neutralised by HPV-18 oncoproteins), they grow without limit.

HeLa cells were the first immortal human cell line. They were taken without Henrietta Lacks's consent. The ethical legacy is still being addressed — her family didn't learn the cells existed until 1973, and only signed an agreement with the NIH on access to her genome in 2013.
items.why: Cell death is taught as inevitable. The cellular machinery to bypass it exists; cancer cells exploit it; HeLa cells made it visible.
